Inspect lower/older leaves for spot pattern
Check the bottom leaves for small spots with yellow margins and larger spots with ring patterns; note where symptoms started.
Whether the visible pattern matches descriptions of ring-forming leaf spots that start low in the canopy.
Which pathogen is present; several diseases share these signs (e.g. target spot and early blight).
Hand-lens check for black fruiting bodies in lesions
Examine lesion centres with a hand lens for tiny black specks (fungal fruiting bodies).
Presence of structures consistent with fruiting bodies of fungi such as the apple or grape black-rot fungi.
The fungal species; fruiting bodies of other or secondary fungi can look similar.
Inspect leaves for mites and eggs
Look on affected leaves for small red adult mites, yellowish nymphs and masses of round eggs.
Whether mites are present on bronzed or webbed leaves.
The mite species (the verified source identifies only the genus Tetranychus).
Check the leaf underside below lesions
Turn affected leaves over and look for white growth or dusty dark/green spore growth below the lesions.
Whether sporulation consistent with downy mildew (white) or leaf blight (dusty fuzz) is visible.
The organism; laboratory examination is needed for identification.
Cross-section of cane/spur below a symptomatic grape shoot
Cut across the cane, spur or cordon from which a symptomatic shoot originates and look for concentric rings of dark spots.
Wood symptoms described for Esca in the verified source.
Which trunk-disease fungus is present; other trunk diseases also discolour wood. Laboratory isolation is required for identification.
Check maize lesion shape against the leaf veins
Note whether lesions are rectangular and bounded by veins with blunt ends, or long cigar-shaped lesions tapering at the ends.
Which description (gray leaf spot vs northern leaf blight) the lesion shape matches.
A confirmed diagnosis; lesion shape can vary with hybrid and stage.
Cut through an apple fruit-rot lesion
Cut through the rot; black rot decay is not cone-shaped (unlike bitter rot) and usually there is one spot per fruit.

Hot, humid tropical crop: optimum 21–36 °C for growth, 25–29 °C at flowering and 20–25 °C at grain formation.
